explanations.answer: Water for the people to drink
explanations.explanation: Water, baker. The verse says it plainly: “They camped at Rephidim, but there was no water for the people to drink.” (Exodus 17:1) A whole congregation of people, and nothing for them to drink. That's a one star review and a very short sentence.

Shade never comes up in this verse, friend. What the text says is that they camped at Rephidim, but there was no water for the people to drink. (Exodus 17:1) That's the missing piece. A little shade would be nice, but nobody can drink shade.

Close, because livestock do show up in this scene. The people mention their livestock in the very next complaints. (Exodus 17:3) But the verse names the missing thing: no water for the people to drink. (Exodus 17:1) Grass isn't mentioned at all.
The LORD. Moses asks, “Why do you test the LORD?” (Exodus 17:2) The people had been contending with Moses, and his question brings the LORD into it. I bet he said it with one eyebrow up, too.

Aaron isn't part of this exchange, baker. Moses' question is, “Why do you test the LORD?” (Exodus 17:2) Aaron doesn't show up until later in the chapter, when he goes up the hill with Moses. (Exodus 17:10) For now it's just Moses and a crowd of thirsty people.

The elders are in this chapter, but not in this question. Moses asks, “Why do you test the LORD?” (Exodus 17:2) The elders show up in verse 5, when the LORD tells Moses to take some of them along. So they come in a little later, and nobody's testing them.

True. They grumble, “Why have you brought us out of Egypt…to make us and our children and livestock die of thirst?” (Exodus 17:3) Notice they bring in the kids and the livestock too. Everybody in camp is part of that complaint.

This one is actually true, friend. The people grumble against Moses: “…to make us and our children and livestock die of thirst?” (Exodus 17:3) They say it out loud, and they include their children and their livestock. When you're thirsty, you ask the biggest question you can think of.

Moses cried out to the LORD. (Exodus 17:4) The whole camp is in his face, and he takes it straight to God. I think that's the right move every time, baker. When the crowd gets loud, go to the One who is already listening.
The text doesn't send Moses looking for Aaron here. It says Moses cried out to the LORD. (Exodus 17:4) He asks, “What should I do with these people?” That's a question for God.

No tent-hiding in this scene. The verse says Moses cried out to the LORD. (Exodus 17:4) He says, “A little more and they will stone me!” I'll admit, if I were him I'd be looking for the nearest door. Moses cries out to the LORD instead.

explanations.answer: The staff he struck the Nile with
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The LORD says, “Take along in your hand the staff with which you struck the Nile, and go.” (Exodus 17:5) Moses already knows this staff, so he doesn't have to go shopping for a new one. Then the LORD says He will stand there before him by the rock at Horeb. (Exodus 17:6) I once kept my own tools close at hand too, because you never know which one the day is going to call for.

explanations.answer: The jar of manna from the camp
explanations.explanation: The jar isn't in this verse, friend. The LORD tells Moses to take the staff with which he struck the Nile. (Exodus 17:5) The manna was the food the LORD gave the people in the desert. (Exodus 16:35) But this trip is about water, and manna wouldn't help with that.

explanations.answer: A horn filled with anointing oil
explanations.explanation: No oil is mentioned here, baker. The LORD says to take the staff with which Moses struck the Nile. (Exodus 17:5) A horn of oil might look impressive on a walk through the desert. But the instructions only ask for a staff.

Strikes, baker! The LORD says, “And when you strike the rock, water will come out of it for the people to drink.” (Exodus 17:6) A rock. In a desert. And water is coming out of it. I've pressed a lot of dough in my day, and not once has a rock given me a drink. The LORD also says He will stand there before Moses by the rock, so Moses isn't doing this alone.

The word in this verse is strike, friend. The LORD says, “And when you strike the rock, water will come out of it for the people to drink.” (Exodus 17:6) Moses isn't asked to talk to it here. Let's not hand the rock a conversation it wasn't invited to.

Anointing isn't part of this one, baker. The LORD says, “And when you strike the rock, water will come out of it for the people to drink.” (Exodus 17:6) It's a strike, plain and simple. I only know oil for greasing my cookie pans, anyway.

It's the other way around, friend. The text says Moses did this “…in the sight of the elders of Israel.” (Exodus 17:6) The LORD had told him to take some of the elders along. (Exodus 17:5) That's a lot of eyes on one rock.

False. Moses struck the rock “…in the sight of the elders of Israel.” (Exodus 17:6) The LORD had told him to take some of the elders along, so they were right there watching. It was a front-row seat to water coming out of a rock.

Quarreled. The verse says Moses named the place that “…because the Israelites quarreled, and because they tested the LORD…” (Exodus 17:7) The text gives two reasons, and quarreling is the first. Some places get named for the view. This one got named for what the people did.

Resting isn't one of the reasons in this verse, baker. Moses named the place because the Israelites quarreled, and because they tested the LORD. (Exodus 17:7) The name points back to the quarreling and the testing.

Prayer isn't the reason given here. The verse says the place was named because the Israelites quarreled, and because they tested the LORD. (Exodus 17:7) Moses is the one who cried out in verse 4. The name is about the people's quarreling.

Joshua, friend! Moses tells him, “Choose some of our men and go out to fight the Amalekites.” (Exodus 17:9) Then the very next verse says Joshua did as Moses had instructed him. (Exodus 17:10) The text gives us the order and then the doing. I wish my mornings were that tidy when I face a full batch of dough.

Caleb is a name from the Bible, baker, but he isn't in this passage. Caleb was one of the men sent to spy out Canaan. (Numbers 13:6) Here, Moses gives the order to Joshua. (Exodus 17:9) Good name to know, just a different story.

Gideon is from much later, friend. His story is in the book of Judges. (Judges 6:11) In this scene, Moses gives the order to Joshua: “Choose some of our men and go out to fight the Amalekites.” (Exodus 17:9) Different era for Gideon, but a good name to know.

Hilltop. Moses says, “Tomorrow I will stand on the hilltop with the staff of God in my hand.” (Exodus 17:9) Joshua is the one told to go out and fight, and Moses takes the hilltop. That hilltop ends up mattering a lot.

No river in this plan, baker. Moses says, “Tomorrow I will stand on the hilltop with the staff of God in my hand.” (Exodus 17:9) The staff did strike the Nile once, but that's a different place. This time it's up high.

Moses isn't on the front line in this plan. He says, “Tomorrow I will stand on the hilltop with the staff of God in my hand.” (Exodus 17:9) Joshua is the one who goes out to fight. Moses takes the hill, and the hill ends up being a big deal.
Holds up his hands. The text says, “As long as Moses held up his hands, Israel prevailed…” (Exodus 17:11) It's an odd thing to hang a battle on, if you ask me. But that's what the verse says.

Kneeling isn't what the verse describes, friend. It says, “As long as Moses held up his hands, Israel prevailed…” (Exodus 17:11) It's all about those hands. Down is not the direction you want them going.

Moses isn't shouting orders down the hill in this verse. It says, “As long as Moses held up his hands, Israel prevailed…” (Exodus 17:11) The verse puts the weight on his hands, not on calling out to Joshua.

explanations.answer: Set a stone under him and hold his hands up
explanations.explanation: Both parts, baker. They “…took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it.” Then Aaron and Hur held his hands up, “…one on each side…” (Exodus 17:12) Moses gets a seat and two helpers. I could have used a Hur or two in my drawer days.

explanations.answer: Take the staff and hold it up themselves
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say they take the staff, friend. It says they put a stone under Moses, and Aaron and Hur held his hands up, one on each side. (Exodus 17:12) The helping happens right there beside him. Nobody swaps places with the staff.

explanations.answer: Run down the hill to help Joshua fight
explanations.explanation: They stay on the hill. The verse says Aaron and Hur held Moses' hands up, one on each side, so his hands remained steady until the sun went down. (Exodus 17:12) Joshua is the one fighting down below. (Exodus 17:10) Their job is right next to Moses.
Side. Aaron and Hur held his hands up, “…one on each side…” (Exodus 17:12) One helper per arm, and both hands stay up. Nobody has to pick a favorite arm.
Sun. Their help kept his hands steady “…until the sun went down.” (Exodus 17:12) That's the end point the verse gives. His hands had grown heavy, so I'm glad he had company, baker.

A stone does show up in this verse, friend, but it isn't the blank. They put a stone under Moses so he could sit on it. (Exodus 17:12) The hands are held up one on each side. The stone is just the seat.
The moon never comes up in this passage. The verse says his hands remained steady “…until the sun went down.” (Exodus 17:12) That's the time marker. The hands held until sundown.

The army is down below with Joshua, not holding Moses' hands. (Exodus 17:10) Aaron and Hur hold his hands up, “…one on each side…” (Exodus 17:12) It takes two people, not a whole army. Sometimes two is plenty.

Reminder. The LORD says, “Write this on a scroll as a reminder and recite it to Joshua…” (Exodus 17:14) So the command is to write it down and say it out loud. Good habit, baker. I keep my recipes written down too.

No song in this verse, baker. The LORD says, “Write this on a scroll as a reminder and recite it to Joshua…” (Exodus 17:14) It's written and spoken, but it isn't a song. Moses didn't have to carry a tune, which is good news for me, since I can't either.

The verse uses a different word. The LORD says, “Write this on a scroll as a reminder and recite it to Joshua…” (Exodus 17:14) It's a reminder, something to keep and remember. It isn't called a warning.

That's it. The LORD says, “…I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.” (Exodus 17:14) The reason for the scroll comes right in the same breath. It's a serious word from the LORD, so I'll just say it plainly and leave it there.

Serving isn't mentioned, friend. The LORD says, “…I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.” (Exodus 17:14) That's the reason He gives for the scroll. It's a heavy line, so let's take it just as written.

explanations.answer: Drive them far into the east
explanations.explanation: No eastward move in this verse, baker. The LORD says, “…I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.” (Exodus 17:14) It's about blotting out the memory, not moving anybody anywhere. A heavy line, and the text says it just that way.

The LORD Is My Banner. Moses built an altar and named it that. (Exodus 17:15) Then he said, “The LORD will war against Amalek from generation to generation.” (Exodus 17:16) The name points straight to the LORD.

That's a real name from the Bible, baker, but it's another story. Abraham named a place The LORD Will Provide. (Genesis 22:14) Here, Moses names his altar The LORD Is My Banner. (Exodus 17:15) Different man, different place.

That one belongs to another altar, friend. Gideon built an altar and called it The LORD Is Peace. (Judges 6:24) Moses' altar here is named The LORD Is My Banner. (Exodus 17:15) Both are good names for an altar.
Not quite, baker. Moses says, “The LORD will war against Amalek from generation to generation.” (Exodus 17:16) That's a lot longer than one generation. The words stretch down the line.
False. Moses says, “The LORD will war against Amalek from generation to generation.” (Exodus 17:16) So it isn't one generation, it reaches down through many. I think the LORD wanted it remembered.
